(3) The district's composition (parts of Wake, Johnston, Lee, Harnett, Franklin, Caswell, Person, and Granville counties) is exurban and leans right. (4) Democrat Paul Barringer is a credible nominee, but no polling or other contrary evidence in the race file suggests the seat is competitive. (5) Third-party candidates (Green and Libertarian) are on the ballot but are not favored to win. Without polling, confidence is medium despite the strong structural indicators.

NC-14 is rated R+15 (Solid Republican) by Cook Political Report under the newly redrawn October 2025 map, and incumbent Tim Moore — a former decade-long Speaker of the North Carolina House — enjoys a strong structural advantage. Without any district-specific general election polling, the district's partisan lean and Moore's incumbency profile make a Republican hold nearly certain.

title: 2026 U.S. Senate election in North Carolina

forecast.rationale: Democrat Roy Cooper holds a significant lead in the sole public poll available, and his strong name recognition as a former governor provides an advantage in this open-seat race. However, North Carolina is a competitive state, and the race is expected to draw substantial outside spending, indicating a potentially closer contest than current polling suggests.

title: North Dakota At-Large U.S. House Election, 2026

forecast.rationale: North Dakota is a deeply Republican state (Trump +35 in 2024), the at-large seat has been held by the GOP since 2011, and incumbent Julie Fedorchak won with ~67% in 2024. Her Democratic-NPL challenger lacks visible campaign infrastructure, while the Republican primary challenger poses no general-election threat.

Incumbent Republican Jim Pillen remains the clear favorite based on Nebraska’s strong recent Republican gubernatorial history, his incumbency, and a large fundraising advantage. The only cited public poll is a single April PPP survey showing Pillen ahead of Democrat Lynne Walz 38%-33% with 12% for Rick Beard and 17% undecided, which suggests a competitive race but still a Republican lead. That poll is early, there is only one numeric poll, and the large undecided share increases uncertainty. Walz appears to be a credible nominee with some fundraising strength, but the broader state and race context still point to a Republican advantage rather than a tossup. The third-party Legal Marijuana NOW candidate could affect the final margin, but an outright non-Republican win remains less likely on the available data.

Incumbent Republican Mike Flood is heavily favored in Nebraska's 1st District, which nonpartisan analysts (Cook, Inside Elections, Sabato's Crystal Ball) uniformly rate as Safe Republican. Flood won re-election in 2024 with 60.1% of the vote and the district's partisan baseline is strongly Republican. Available polling is limited to two Democratic-leaning firms (Tavern Research and Zenith Research), which modestly reduces confidence, but all three survey matchups show Flood leading Democrat Chris Backemeyer. Ahlman (I) remains a wild card as he works to secure ballot access, and Sandman (L) is a minor factor. District fundamentals and incumbency strongly favor a Republican hold.

This open-seat race for Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District is one of the most competitive House seats in the country, but structural fundamentals give Democrats a modest edge. The district (Omaha's 'blue dot') voted Democratic in the last two presidential elections, and Republican Don Bacon's retirement removes the GOP incumbency advantage that had historically allowed ticket-splitting. Cook Political Report rates the race Lean Democratic as of mid-2026. Democrat Denise Powell won a competitive primary against state senator John Cavanaugh, while Republican Brinker Harding ran unopposed with an endorsement from President Trump. Harding is a credible, well-funded candidate with city council experience, and the district has repeatedly shown willingness to elect Republicans down ballot despite its presidential lean. No public general election polls exist for this matchup, so the forecast relies entirely on structural signals and ratings — hence low confidence. The Democratic advantage is real but limited rather than commanding, consistent with a lean Democratic rating.

Nebraska's 3rd District has a Cook PVI of R+27 and incumbent Adrian Smith has won each of his ten re-election bids with over 70% of the vote, making a Republican hold virtually certain despite the absence of public polling. The fragmented opposition field — a Democratic first-time candidate, a third-party nominee, and two independents — faces steep structural headwinds in one of the most Republican-leaning districts in the country.

Nebraska's strong Republican lean and Ricketts' incumbency provide a significant advantage. While Dan Osborn has shown some competitiveness, the lack of recent polling and the Democratic candidate's stated intention to withdraw solidify the Republican's position.

Incumbent Republican Kelly Ayotte holds a consistent advantage in the available candidate-level general-election polling, leading Democrat Cinde Warmington by 8 points in an April 2026 UNH poll and by 7 points in a March 2026 Saint Anselm poll. Ayotte also won the 2024 open-seat race with 53.6%, and New Hampshire has recently been willing to elect Republican governors even while remaining competitive at the presidential level. That said, this is still a swing-state environment and the polling record is fairly sparse, with only two directly relevant Ayotte-Warmington surveys, so the race should not be rated stronger than Lean Republican. Minor-party and independent candidates are on the ballot, but the available data still points to a Republican edge in the major-party contest.

No general-election polling exists for this open-seat race as of June 2026; all polls listed pertain only to the Democratic primary and lack usable head-to-head matchups. The district is a classic swing seat — Harris carried it by roughly 2 points in 2024 — and the departure of incumbent Democrat Chris Pappas (running for Senate) removes any incumbency advantage. The Democratic primary features a well-funded field (Maura Sullivan raised over $2.6M, Stefany Shaheen brings high name recognition) while the GOP primary has two credible but less nationally prominent candidates. However, without any head-to-head polling or a clear general-election nominee from either party, structural uncertainty is very high. The seat is best classified as a tossup with only a marginal Democratic lean based on the district's recent presidential performance.

No public general-election polling exists, so this is a fundamentals-based forecast. Incumbent Democrat Maggie Goodlander won the open seat narrowly (52%) in 2024 and benefits from incumbency and the district's Democratic lean, but the Republican field is unsettled ahead of the September 8 primary and national House control is expected to be closely divided.

title: 2026 U.S. Senate election in New Hampshire

forecast.rationale: Christopher Pappas consistently leads John E. Sununu in general election matchups across four polls from January to April 2026, with an average margin of approximately 3 percentage points. However, all available polling is now several months old, and the race remains competitive in a swing state.

title: 2026 U.S. House Election in New Jersey's 1st Congressional District

forecast.rationale: No district-specific general-election polls exist, limiting granular confidence. However, the race fundamentals overwhelmingly favor Democrats: NJ-01 is a heavily Democratic district with a 44% to 19% Democratic registration advantage; incumbent Donald Norcross has held the seat since 2014 with strong union and labor ties; and all major nonpartisan forecasters (Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, Sabato's Crystal Ball) rate the race as Solid/Safe Democratic. Republican challenger Damon Galdo is a first-time general-election nominee who failed to secure the nomination in his two prior primary attempts. With no contrary evidence in the supplied data, Democrats remain prohibitive favorites.

No public general-election polls exist for this matchup (only a reference to internal Democratic polling with no released numbers). With zero numeric polling data, the forecast relies on race fundamentals. Van Drew is a four-term incumbent with a slight Republican voter registration edge in the district, making him a narrow favorite. However, he is a party-switcher (elected as a Democrat in 2018, switched in 2019), which may complicate his coalition. Democratic nominee Zack Mullock is a credible challenger—two-term mayor of Cape May with executive experience—and won a competitive four-way primary on June 2, 2026, suggesting Democratic enthusiasm. The race is described as Democrats' best flip opportunity in years, with low Trump approval ratings cited as a potential headwind for Van Drew, a close Trump ally. The combination of incumbent advantage and registration edge vs. a credible challenger and unfavorable national environment suggests a narrow Republican edge, but the absence of polling makes this highly uncertain.

title: 2026 U.S. House Election for New Jersey's 3rd Congressional District

forecast.rationale: A D+5 PVI district that delivered an 8-point win for Kamala Harris in 2024, combined with a "Solid D" rating from Cook Political Report, gives first-term incumbent Herb Conaway a commanding structural advantage despite no public polling being available.

No public general-election polling exists for this race, which limits direct voter measurement and reduces confidence. However, structural indicators overwhelmingly favor Republicans. The district has a Cook PVI of R+14, approximately 40% of registered voters are Republican, and the race is rated 'Solid R' by Cook. Chris Smith is a 45-year incumbent seeking a 24th term and is described as heavily favored. Rachel Peace is a first-time challenger in a heavily Republican district without significant independent spending or polling evidence of a shift. Absent contrary data, the most likely outcome is a decisive Republican hold with a large margin.

title: 2026 U.S. House of Representatives Election for New Jersey's 5th Congressional District

forecast.rationale: No public race-specific polling exists as of mid-2026, reducing confidence below 'high.' However, the structural race data strongly favors Democrats: incumbent Josh Gottheimer (first elected 2016) is seeking a sixth term; the district has a Democratic voter registration edge (35% Democratic vs. 26% Republican); Cook Political Report rates the race as Solid Democratic; and Gottheimer is a well-funded, prominent moderate who co-chairs the bipartisan Problem Solvers Caucus. Republican Sean Kirrane is a credible candidate with a business background and a socially moderate pitch, but faces a steep structural climb in a Democratic-leaning district with a strong incumbent. Independent Adam Rueda lacks the resources or profile to seriously compete. Given the incumbency, registration advantage, and national rating, Democrats hold an overwhelming advantage, consistent with a safe_d rating (~95%+ win probability). The lack of direct polling, however, keeps confidence at medium.

No public general-election polling is available for this race, which limits confidence. However, structural indicators are overwhelming: the district has roughly a 2-to-1 Democratic voter registration advantage, Cook Political Report rates it Solidly Democratic, and 38-year incumbent Frank Pallone Jr. (Ranking Member on House Energy and Commerce Committee) enjoys deep name recognition against a first-time Republican challenger. The combination of extreme partisan lean, long incumbency, and no evidence of competitive dynamics makes this a safe Democratic hold with a wide expected margin.

title: 2026 U.S. House of Representatives Election for New Jersey's 7th Congressional District

forecast.rationale: This is a highly competitive race with very sparse data. The only identified poll (June 2026, from a Democratic-aligned source) shows Rebecca Bennett ahead of incumbent Thomas Kean Jr. by 4 points (47%-43%), suggesting genuine vulnerability for the two-term Republican. However, with only one partisan-aligned poll and no independent or GOP polling available, the polling picture is incomplete. The district has a slight Republican voter registration edge, and Kean is an incumbent, but his prolonged absence from Congress since March 2026 due to an undisclosed medical condition is a significant liability that has eroded his incumbency advantage. National analysts have shifted the race to 'Lean R' or 'Toss Up.' Bennett has strong fundraising ($2.7M without corporate PAC money) and a compelling personal story. On balance, the district's underlying Republican tilt gives Kean a narrow edge, but the race is highly uncertain and could easily flip given the sparse data and unusual circumstances.

NJ-08 is a heavily Democratic district with a 52-point Democratic voter registration advantage. No Republican candidate qualified for the primary ballot; instead, GOP county chairs are backing independent Aristotle Eliopoulos, a teacher and union official. Incumbent Democrat Rob Menendez won his June 2026 primary decisively with ~68.8% of the vote. All major nonpartisan forecasters (Cook, Inside Elections, Sabato's) rate the seat Safe/Solid Democratic. While there is no district-specific general election polling, the structural fundamentals overwhelmingly favor the Democratic incumbent. The independent and third-party candidates (Eliopoulos, Honts, Hughey) face severe headwinds in a district where Democrats hold a voter registration advantage of more than 2-to-1. The most likely outcome is a comfortable Democratic hold in the 30+ point margin range.

No district-specific public polling exists, so this forecast relies entirely on non-polling indicators and carries low confidence. Incumbent Democrat Nellie Pou holds the advantages of incumbency and extensive legislative experience, and the race is rated 'Lean Democratic' by Cook Political Report. However, the district is described as markedly more competitive and narrowly backed Donald Trump in the 2024 presidential election, indicating a genuine Republican opportunity. Republican nominee Rosie Pino is a credible challenger with local elected experience, and an independent anti-abortion candidate (Terrisa Bukovinac) is on the ballot. The independent may draw slightly more votes from the Republican-leaning anti-abortion bloc, which could marginally advantage Pou. With zero polls, uncertainty is substantial, supporting a Lean Democratic forecast with low confidence and a narrow single-digit margin.

No public district-specific polls exist for the 2026 NJ-10 race, limiting confidence. However, the structural fundamentals are overwhelmingly Democratic: the district has a 54% Democratic voter registration advantage versus just 10% Republican, covering heavily Democratic urban areas (Newark, East Orange, Irvington, parts of Jersey City). Incumbent Democrat LaMonica McIver already won the seat in a 2024 special election and the 2024 general election by wide margins. Challenger Carmen Bucco is a perennial Republican candidate who has lost multiple prior races for various offices and ran unopposed in the primary, demonstrating minimal party investment. Given the massive registration gap, incumbency advantage, and lack of any polling suggesting competitiveness, a Democratic hold is all but certain.

title: New Jersey's 11th Congressional District Regular Election, 2026

forecast.rationale: No public polling exists for this race, limiting statistical confidence. However, the strongest available signal is the April 2026 special election — a head-to-head matchup between the same two candidates just two months ago — which Mejia won by 21 points (60%–39%). She then won her Democratic primary with approximately 82% of the vote, while Hathaway was unopposed in the GOP primary. The district has a recent history of Democratic representation under Mikie Sherrill. Against the same opponent in the same district, the 21-point special election margin provides a meaningful baseline, but special election turnout may differ from general election turnout, and the lack of polling reduces certainty. The rating of Likely Democratic reflects a clear advantage for Mejia without reaching the Safe threshold.

No independent general-election polls exist for this race as of June 2026. The forecast relies entirely on district fundamentals: New Jersey's 12th Congressional District is rated Solid D by Cook Political Report and has been held by a Democrat since 2015. The district's strong Democratic lean (covering parts of Mercer, Middlesex, Somerset, and Union counties) provides a high baseline advantage. Democratic nominee Adam Hamawy won a competitive 13-candidate primary with 27.4% of the vote, while Republican Gregg Mele — a seven-time prior candidate who has never won elected office — ran unopposed in the GOP primary. The open-seat nature and complete absence of polling reduce confidence, but the district's partisan fundamentals overwhelmingly favor the Democratic candidate. A safe Democratic rating with ~96% win probability is appropriate.

title: 2026 U.S. Senate election in New Jersey

forecast.rationale: New Jersey is a reliably Democratic state, and incumbent Cory Booker has high name recognition. The lack of public polling, however, introduces significant uncertainty.

This is an open-seat race with no general-election head-to-head polling available, which materially increases uncertainty. Still, the available race context gives Democrats an edge: New Mexico has trended Democratic in recent presidential elections, Democrats currently hold the governorship, and Deb Haaland enters the general election as a prominent statewide figure after serving as U.S. Secretary of the Interior and winning her primary decisively. Gregg Hull appears to be a credible Republican nominee with executive experience as Rio Rancho mayor, so the race is not out of reach for Republicans, especially in an open-seat contest centered on crime, the economy, and education. With no direct general-election polling, this forecast relies primarily on state partisan lean, candidate profile, and the overall race description rather than measured voter preference.

title: 2026 U.S. House election for New Mexico's 1st Congressional District

forecast.rationale: No public polling exists for this race. However, structural indicators are overwhelmingly favorable for Democrats: incumbent Rep. Melanie Stansbury won re-election in 2024 with 56.4% of the vote (a ~13-point margin), nonpartisan forecasters rate the district 'Solid D,' and the incumbent has held the seat since 2021. The Republican challenger, Ndidiamaka 'Didi' Okpareke, is a political newcomer (pharmacist and small business owner) with no prior elected office. The district (central New Mexico, including most of Albuquerque) has been reliably Democratic in recent cycles. Given the strong and consistent structural evidence—incumbency, previous margin, and nonpartisan rating—confidence is high despite the absence of current polling.

title: New Mexico's 2nd Congressional District General Election, 2026

forecast.rationale: NM-02 is a highly competitive swing district that Democrat Gabe Vasquez has held by narrow margins since flipping it in 2022. Only one public poll is available — a Republican-aligned NRCC survey from late April 2026 showing Vasquez at 43% and Cunningham at 41%, essentially tied within the margin of error. Vasquez benefits from two-term incumbency, name recognition, and a track record of winning in this district, while Republican nominee Greg Cunningham has lost two prior state legislative races. National handicappers rate the race Lean D to Toss Up, reflecting the district's competitiveness. However, with just one partisan-sponsored poll and no independent or Democratic surveys available, the evidence base is thin enough that uncertainty is high. Democrats hold a narrow advantage due to incumbency and recent electoral performance, but the race remains highly fluid.

Incumbent Teresa Leger Fernandez holds a D+3 district with three-term incumbency advantage, and nonpartisan forecasters rate the seat Solid D. The absence of public polling and the challenger's credible state legislative background caution against a safe rating, but the structural fundamentals clearly favor the Democrat.

title: 2026 U.S. Senate election in New Mexico

forecast.rationale: Incumbent Sen. Ben Ray Luján is a well-known statewide Democrat seeking reelection in a state that has voted Democratic in every presidential election since 2004. The Republican Party lacks a standard ballot nominee and is fielding only a write-in candidate, making this one of the most lopsided Senate race structures in the 2026 cycle.

Nevada is a closely divided swing state, and the available public polling shows an essentially tied race between incumbent Republican Joe Lombardo and Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford. Three candidate-level polls/averages listed here show Lombardo up 1 point, tied, and tied, while the RealClearPolitics average also shows a margin of just 0.5 points. That polling supports no clear favorite. Lombardo gets a slight edge because he is the incumbent and appears to have a substantial fundraising advantage, but those factors are not enough to move the race out of tossup given Nevada’s narrow statewide margins and the consistently razor-close polling. Confidence is only medium because the polling is still limited and early for a 2026 general election.

No district-specific general-election polls exist for NV-01 as of mid-2026, so this forecast relies on non-polling indicators and carries medium confidence. Democratic incumbent Dina Titus has held the seat since 2013 and won re-election with 52.0% in 2024—a solid but not commanding margin in a district that has become more competitive. Republican Carrie Buck is a credible challenger who flipped a state Senate seat from D to R in 2020 and is described as well-funded; she could keep the race close. However, outside race ratings from Cook (Likely D), Sabato's Crystal Ball (Likely D), and Inside Elections (Lean D) all favor Democrats, and Titus's long incumbency and experience provide a structural advantage. The presence of four nonpartisan candidates is unlikely to materially shift the two-party contest. With no polling data to sharpen the estimate, a 'likely D' rating (Democratic win probability ~80%) and a moderate single-digit margin reflect the best assessment of the available information.

No public general-election polls exist for this race, so the forecast relies entirely on structural and historical factors. Nevada's 2nd District has a Cook PVI of R+7, and Donald Trump carried it by 14 points in 2024 — a strong recent Republican baseline. The district has never elected a Democrat to Congress. However, this is an open-seat contest due to Rep. Mark Amodei's retirement, and Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson is a credible recruit with state legislative leadership experience. Republican David Flippo won a crowded primary with Trump's endorsement and ran on a conservative platform. Without polling to test the race's competitiveness, the district's underlying partisanship makes Flippo the clear favorite, but Benitez-Thompson's profile and the open-seat nature prevent this from being rated safe. Confidence is medium due to the absence of any public polling data.

Three-term Democratic incumbent Susie Lee has repeatedly proven her crossover appeal in this swing district, winning by 2.8 points in 2024 even as Trump carried the seat. Republican nominee Marty O'Donnell is a high-profile first-time candidate with Trump's endorsement, but his lack of political experience and short tenure in Nevada give Lee a meaningful structural advantage in a district that remains genuinely competitive.

No general-election head-to-head polls exist for NV-04 (based_on_poll_count=0), so confidence is medium and the forecast relies on race fundamentals and external ratings rather than direct polling. The Cook Political Report rates the race as 'Likely D.' Democratic incumbent Steven Horsford is a well-established four-term congressman with a strong political profile (former state senate Majority Leader, chaired the Congressional Black Caucus, sits on Ways & Means). He has repeatedly demonstrated the ability to outperform the district's presidential lean: Kamala Harris carried NV-04 by just 2 points in 2024, while Horsford outperformed her by roughly 5 points. Republican nominee Cody Whipple, a rancher and small business owner with no prior elected office, won a three-way GOP primary on June 9, 2026, with nearly 62% — a solid but unexceptional primary showing for a non-incumbent. The district's blend of suburban Clark County and rural central Nevada counties keeps it competitive at the presidential level, but Horsford's incumbency, fundraising network, and track record of overperformance give Democrats a clear advantage. An informational Likely Democratic forecast is appropriate, with modest uncertainty due to the complete absence of head-to-head polling data.

title: 2026 U.S. House election in New York's 4th Congressional District

forecast.rationale: No district-specific public polling exists in the race data, and the candidate list includes only incumbent Democrat Laura Gillen (former Hempstead town supervisor, in office since Jan. 2025), with Republican Anthony D'Esposito widely expected but not formally announced. NY-04 is described as a politically competitive Nassau County district, and the race is expected to be a rematch of the 2024 contest Gillen won narrowly, suggesting a closely divided electorate. Gillen's incumbency provides a modest structural edge, but the absence of polling and the lack of a formally listed major-party challenger reduce confidence. The forecast reflects a narrow Democratic advantage consistent with a competitive district where Gillen holds the seat, but the margin of error is large and the race could shift to tossup as more information emerges.

Incumbent Democrat Kathy Hochul benefits from New York's strong Democratic lean and incumbency advantage, but the 2022 race against Lee Zeldin was unexpectedly close (6-point margin), and the description notes recent Republican gains in local offices, creating meaningful uncertainty.

Incumbent Rep. Nick LaLota (R) is seeking a third term in a district Cook Political Report rates as Solid Republican. He won re-election in 2024 with 55.5% of the vote, a clear but not overwhelming margin. The only available poll is a single nonpartisan-grade survey from December 2025 commissioned by a Democratic-aligned group (House Majority PAC), showing LaLota ahead of Democrat Chris Gallant 41%-38% with 20% undecided — suggesting potential competitiveness but with notable caveats: the poll is 6 months old, sponsor-aligned, and taken before the Democratic nominee was determined. The Democratic primary (June 23, 2026) is still 3 days away, with two candidates (Chris Gallant and Lukas Ventouras) competing; the eventual nominee's strength is unknown. With only 1 poll from a partisan source, a large undecided share, and an unsettled general election field, there is meaningful uncertainty. However, LaLota's incumbency, his 55.5% performance in 2024, the district's Republican lean in recent cycles, and the Cook rating all point to a clear Republican advantage — enough for a 'likely_r' rating (roughly 80-94% range) rather than safe_r, but not narrow enough for a tossup or lean given available evidence.

No independent public district-level polls exist for NY-02 as of June 2026, so this forecast relies entirely on structural indicators. The district has a Cook Partisan Voting Index of R+6 and nonpartisan analysts rate the race as 'Solid Republican.' Incumbent Andrew Garbarino has held the seat since 2020 and chairs the House Homeland Security Committee. His moderate, occasionally bipartisan record may help retain crossover support in this Long Island district. Democratic nominee Patrick Halpin is a former Suffolk County Executive and a credible local figure, which prevents the race from being a pure safe seat, but he faces an uphill race in a district that leans 6 points more Republican than the national average. Without any district-level polling, confidence remains medium. The rating of 'likely_r' (approximately 90% Republican win probability) reflects a clear but not overwhelming Republican advantage, factoring in incumbency, the R+6 lean, and Halpin's local stature.

Incumbent Tom Suozzi holds an edge in this competitive Long Island swing seat, having won the 2024 general election by 3.6 points (51.8%) and the February 2024 special election. Cook Political Report's Lean Democratic rating and the absence of any general election polling leave fundamentals — incumbency, Suozzi's demonstrated crossover appeal, and a midterm environment with a Republican president favoring the out-party — as the primary signals.

title: 2026 U.S. House of Representatives election for New York's 5th Congressional District

forecast.rationale: No public polling is available for this race (based_on_poll_count: 0), which reduces confidence to medium. However, all structural indicators point to an overwhelmingly Democratic outcome: Cook PVI D+24 (one of the most Democratic districts nationally), 28-year incumbent Gregory Meeks chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee and won the 2024 general election with 72.9% of the vote, his primary challenger was disqualified clearing his path to renomination, the district has not elected a Republican since the 1990s, and the three Republican primary candidates have limited biographical and campaign profiles publicly available. Given the combination of extreme partisan lean, long incumbency, and weak opposition field, a Democratic win is virtually certain barring extraordinary circumstances, consistent with a safe_d rating and ~98% win probability.

Democrats hold a structural advantage in this D+6 district, and incumbent Grace Meng has won re-election by double digits since 2012, most recently 60.7% in 2024. No public polling exists, and the 24-point pro-Trump swing in the 2024 presidential result adds some uncertainty, but the Cook Political Report rates the seat 'Solid D' and the Republican field is weak, making a Democratic hold the heavily likely outcome.

This open-seat race is in New York's 7th Congressional District, described as a solidly Democratic, progressive stronghold, making the Democratic nominee heavily favored in the general election regardless of the primary outcome. The only available poll (Emerson College, May 2026) surveys the Democratic primary — not the general election — and shows a close contest between Claire Valdez (23%) and Antonio Reynoso (21%), with Julie Won at 13%, Vichal Kumar at 1%, and a very large 43% undecided. With the Democratic primary just three days away (June 23, 2026), the nominee remains genuinely unsettled, but the district's strong Democratic lean means the eventual nominee will have an overwhelming advantage over Republican Melvin Rivera, who advanced unopposed. No general-election polling exists, so confidence is medium. The margin estimate reflects the typical Democratic performance in this deep-blue seat.

New York's 8th Congressional District is overwhelmingly Democratic, with major nonpartisan forecasters rating it "Safe D." Incumbent Hakeem Jeffries is the House Minority Leader and has represented the district since 2013, giving him enormous structural advantages in name recognition, fundraising, and institutional support. The only identified polling is a private October 2025 survey showing Jeffries with a 50-point lead over primary challenger Chi Ossé. No general election polling exists because the race is broadly viewed as noncompetitive. Two Republican candidates (Lewis Mizrahi and Richard Simmons) have limited public profiles in this heavily Democratic district covering central Brooklyn. The Democratic primary on June 23, 2026 — three days from now — is the de facto competitive contest, but Jeffries' incumbency and leadership position make his nomination nearly certain. In the general election, Democrats hold an overwhelming advantage. Confidence is set to medium because the forecast relies on structural district characteristics and candidate strength rather than direct public general-election polling.

NY-09's D+22 Cook PVI makes a Democratic general election victory all but certain regardless of nominee. The decisive contest is the Democratic primary, where longtime incumbent Yvette Clarke (serving since 2006) faces two challengers but benefits from deep institutional support and name recognition in a district she has represented for nearly two decades.

NY-10 is a safely Democratic seat where the general election is a formality — the Democratic nominee will almost certainly prevail (Goldman won 81.0% in 2024, and the Republican candidate Jennifer Moore is a long-shot who advanced without appearing on the primary ballot). The real contest is the June 23 Democratic primary, just 3 days from now. Two polls (Emerson College June 2026, Demand Progress Sept. 2025) show Brad Lander leading incumbent Daniel Goldman among likely Democratic primary voters. Accordingly, Lander is the current informational favorite to become the Democratic nominee and general election winner. Confidence is medium rather than high because the poll matchups lack numeric toplines in the available data, and one of the two polls is from September 2025, making it relatively old for a competitive primary.

No public NY-11 general-election polls exist as of June 2026, so the forecast relies entirely on structural and contextual signals. Nicole Malliotakis is the three-term incumbent Republican in a district described as having trended conservative; it remains the only Republican-held U.S. House seat in New York City. The district's existing boundaries were upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court in early 2026, preserving the current configuration rather than shifting to a more Democratic-leaning map. Michael DeCillis is the sole active Democratic candidate and has a compelling personal story (former NYPD, 9/11 first responder, attorney), but no polling, fundraising data, or public evidence of a competitive race is available. Major nonpartisan forecasters rate the contest Likely Republican or Solid Republican. Without district-specific polling, the race falls at the lower end of the "likely Republican" band—reflecting a clear Republican structural advantage but tempered by the absence of direct voter data and the distinct possibility that a well-funded Democratic challenger could narrow the margin in a general election environment.

NY-12 is an open seat following Rep. Jerrold Nadler's retirement, but the district (Manhattan's Upper West Side and Midtown East) is one of the most reliably Democratic in the country (Cook PVI: Solid/Safe D). The Republican nominee Caroline Shinkle is a non-factor in a district where Democratic candidates routinely win by 50+ points, regardless of which candidate emerges from the competitive 10-person Democratic primary on June 23.

No Republican candidates filed and the district (D+32) has not elected a Republican since 1970, making the Democratic primary winner virtually certain to win the general election. At the candidate level, five-term incumbent Adriano Espaillat is the likely primary winner against four challengers, but the absence of any polling data and the presence of credible progressive challengers (one endorsed by NYC Mayor Mamdani) introduces uncertainty into the primary outcome.

NY-14 is a heavily Democratic Bronx/Queens district where Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez won 68.9% in 2024. She has nearly $15 million cash on hand versus negligible primary challenger funds (~$8k and ~$4k) and faces a structurally weak Republican opponent in a district where a Democratic hold is virtually certain.

title: 2026 U.S. House election for New York's 15th Congressional District

forecast.rationale: NY-15 has a Cook PVI of D+27 and is described as a heavily Democratic South Bronx district where the Democratic primary is effectively the decisive contest. The Democratic primary is three days away (June 23, 2026) and is competitive between incumbent Ritchie Torres, Michael Blake, and Jose Vega. Regardless of which Democrat emerges, the general election strongly favors the Democratic nominee given the district's partisan makeup. The Republican (Stylo A. Sapaskis) advanced without a primary and the independent (Andre Easton) faces long odds. Zero general-election polls exist. Confidence is medium rather than high because the primary outcome is uncertain and could affect turnout dynamics or margin, though not the overall party winner. The margin estimate of 45 points reflects typical D+27 district performance.

However, this is an open seat (incumbent Nancy Mace running for governor) with both party nominations still unresolved as of the June 23 runoffs, which introduces substantial uncertainty. The 86% Republican win probability reflects a clear but not overwhelming GOP lean; a 9-point margin is a plausible estimate for a district drawn to favor Republicans without incumbency. Confidence is low due to the absence of any polling data.

No general election polling exists for this race. The forecast relies on structural indicators: incumbent Rep. Joe Wilson (first elected 2001) won his 2026 Republican primary decisively with 74.2% of the vote. Democrats have not yet finalized a nominee as of June 20, with a primary runoff scheduled for June 23. The district is rated 'Solid Republican' by the Cook Political Report and covers Lexington County plus portions of Richland, Aiken, Barnwell, and Orangeburg counties — a strongly Republican-leaning jurisdiction. A third-party Workers Party candidate is also on the ballot but does not appear competitive from available data. Given incumbency, no competitive general election signals, the district's partisan baseline, and zero polling, a Safe Republican rating with medium confidence is appropriate.

South Carolina's 3rd District is the most conservative in the state, has not elected a Democrat to Congress in decades, and now features a Republican incumbent, Sheri Biggs, seeking her first full term. With zero general-election polling available, the forecast relies on these fundamentals, which point to an overwhelming Republican advantage.

Incumbent William Timmons represents a reliably Republican Upstate district (Cook Solid Republican, recent margins of 30–40 points) and won his primary decisively with Trump's endorsement. Without any general-election polling or evidence of a shifted environment, the structural fundamentals overwhelmingly favor Timmons.

No public general-election polling exists for this race as of mid-June 2026. The forecast therefore relies on structural factors: the district is a Republican stronghold held by the GOP since 2010, outgoing Rep. Ralph Norman won 63.5% in 2024, and nonpartisan forecasters (e.g., Cook Political Report) rate the seat as Solidly Republican. Republican nominee Wes Climer is a sitting state senator who faced no primary opposition. Democratic nominee Mallory Dittmer won a competitive primary with 55.8%, but the district's heavy Republican lean gives Climer an overwhelming advantage. The open-seat status and absence of polling reduce confidence below high, but the structural data strongly supports a safe Republican hold.

Clyburn's 34-year incumbency, 90.3% primary performance, and the district's Solidly Democratic rating under current lines (a GOP redistricting effort failed in May 2026) point to a near-certain Democratic hold. No general election polls exist, but the structural partisan lean and challenger weakness are decisive.

There are no public general-election polls for this race. The forecast relies on structural factors: Cook Political Report rates the district 'Solid Republican,' the district has not elected a Democrat to Congress in the modern era, and incumbent Russell Fry won 65% of the vote in 2024. Democratic challenger John Vincent is a credible nominee with a compelling personal story, but faces an extremely difficult partisan environment in this heavily Republican district. The absence of polling reduces confidence from high to medium, but the available race data points to an overwhelming Republican advantage.

title: 2026 U.S. Senate election in South Carolina

The GOP is favored to retain the office regardless of whether incumbent Larry Rhoden or runoff challenger Toby Doeden is the eventual nominee, and Rhoden is provisionally listed as the predicted winner because he is the incumbent and remains in the runoff. title: United States Senate election in South Dakota, 2026

forecast.rationale: Incumbent Republican Mike Rounds is running for re-election in a state that strongly favors Republicans. There is no polling data available, but South Dakota has a consistent history of electing Republican candidates to statewide office.

This is an open-seat race, but the available race data still points strongly to Republicans. Tennessee has not elected a Democrat statewide since 2006, and the race description says the general election is heavily Republican-favored. Within the GOP primary, Marsha Blackburn appears dominant: she leads all available Republican primary polls by very large margins, has strong statewide name recognition, major endorsements, and a substantial fundraising edge. The Democratic field appears weaker and less established statewide. Confidence is not high because the available polling is primary polling only, not general-election polling, and the election is still months away; however, the state’s recent statewide partisan track record and the current candidate field support a safe Republican informational forecast.

No public polling exists for this race, which necessarily suppresses confidence. However, the structural evidence is exceptionally strong: the district is described as heavily Republican, has not elected a Democrat to Congress since the 19th century, and all major election forecasters rate it a Safe/Solid Republican seat. The May 2026 redistricting left the 1st District largely intact. Incumbent Republican Diana Harshbarger (seeking a fourth term) benefits from incumbency, name recognition, and a district with a deeply entrenched GOP lean. The Democratic primary field consists of three first-time candidates (Kristi Burke, Hernan H. Garcia, David S. Kerr Jr.) who will compete in an August 6 primary against each other, and four independent candidates are also on the general election ballot — none show evidence in the provided data of fundraising or organizational strength sufficient to meaningfully contest the seat. Given the district's partisan composition and historical voting patterns, an overwhelming Republican advantage is virtually certain even though no direct polling corroboration exists.

Incumbent Tim Burchett has won each re-election since 2019 with over 69% of the vote in a district rated Safe/Solid Republican by all major nonpartisan forecasters. No public polling exists, but the district's fundamental partisan makeup and Burchett's consistent performance make a Democratic or independent victory highly unlikely.

No polling data exists for this race. The forecast relies entirely on structural indicators. Chuck Fleischmann is an eight-term Republican incumbent (first elected 2010), chairs a prominent House Appropriations subcommittee, and faces no primary challenge, signaling strong party and institutional support. The Democratic field is unsettled — two relatively unknown candidates (Golladay and Martin) are competing in an August 6 primary, meaning no Democratic nominee will be known for another six weeks. Five independent candidates are on the general election ballot, including two with Republican backgrounds (Arnold and Howard-Hill), which could fragment the anti-Fleischmann vote further. The district was redrawn in May 2026 under a new map passed by the Republican-controlled Tennessee legislature; the race description notes 'newly competitive dynamics' but without partisan composition data or polling, the net effect is uncertain. Historically, Tennessee's 3rd has been a safe Republican seat (Fleischmann won by ~19 points in 2024). The combination of entrenched incumbency, no primary opposition, a fragmented Democratic field (still in primary phase), and a map drawn by a Republican legislature points to a very strong Republican advantage. However, the absence of any polling and the recency of redistricting limit confidence, and the margin estimate of ~24 points is a placeholder based on historical performance without survey data to confirm.

No public polling exists in the race data; this forecast is based entirely on structural and candidate factors. The district has a Cook PVI of R+11, and incumbent Scott DesJarlais is a long-serving Republican seeking an eighth term after winning his party's nomination. However, the district has been redrawn to include more urban Nashville voters, which may somewhat shift the baseline. The Democratic field is unsettled — four candidates are competing in the August 6, 2026 primary, so no general election opponent is yet known, adding uncertainty. An independent candidate is also on the ballot. Given the strong GOP structural advantage but absent polling, unresolved Democratic nomination, and redistricting uncertainty, the most defensible rating is Likely Republican with a somewhat tempered win probability.

No public polling exists for this race, which limits confidence. However, major election forecasters rate this seat as Solid/Safe Republican under the dramatically redrawn map that removed heavily Democratic Davidson County (Nashville) and stretches into more rural/suburban territory. The structural partisan lean of the new district overwhelmingly favors Republicans. Incumbent Andy Ogles faces a primary challenge from Charlie Hatcher, and Democrats have a competitive multi-candidate primary, but neither primary introduces evidence sufficient to overcome the district's strong Republican baseline. The general election is not expected to be competitive under the current map configuration.

No public polling exists for this race. The general election nominees are undetermined (primaries are August 6, 2026), the district was redrawn in May 2026 via mid-cycle redistricting, and the seat is open — all of which introduce meaningful uncertainty. However, structural fundamentals are overwhelmingly Republican: Cook PVI R+13 and a 27-point Trump margin. In a district this partisan, the Republican nominee — whoever emerges from a competitive four-way primary — is a very strong favorite in the general election. The mid-cycle redistricting could alter the precise partisan composition but is unlikely to flip the district's fundamental character. The absence of polling and the fluid candidate environment preclude high confidence, but the underlying partisan lean clearly supports a Safe Republican rating with an estimated double-digit general election margin.

title: 2026 U.S. House of Representatives election for Tennessee's 7th Congressional District

forecast.rationale: No public general-election polling exists for this race, so the forecast relies entirely on structural indicators. Those indicators strongly favor Republicans: the district backed Donald Trump by over 20 points in 2024; Cook Political Report, Inside Elections, and Sabato's Crystal Ball all rate it Safe/Solid Republican; and incumbent Republican Matt Van Epps already holds the seat after winning the December 2025 special election. The mid-decade redistricting (May 2026) and ongoing court challenge to the map introduce some uncertainty, as does the fact that the August 6 primaries have not yet occurred (leaving the Democratic nominee and independent candidates still undetermined). However, no evidence in the provided data suggests a general-election environment that would overcome the district's strong Republican lean. On the current map and available information, Republicans hold an overwhelming advantage.

No district-specific polling exists for this race (zero polls found as of June 2026), so confidence is capped at medium and the forecast relies entirely on structural indicators. Those indicators strongly favor the incumbent Republican: (1) Cook Political Report rates the redrawn district as 'Solid R'; (2) the race description explicitly states the district 'still leans heavily Republican'; (3) incumbent David Kustoff is seeking a sixth term with a long tenure and a House Ways and Means Committee seat; (4) four Democrats are competing in an August 6 primary, meaning no unified Democratic challenger has emerged yet, and no Democratic candidate has demonstrated fundraising or name recognition sufficient to suggest a competitive general election; (5) six independent candidates are on the ballot without evidence of significant organization or support. The May 2026 redraw added more of Shelby County (Memphis), which could modestly reduce the Republican margin compared to the previous configuration, but the available data do not indicate the district became competitive. A margin of roughly 20-25 points is consistent with a safe Republican seat of this profile. Given the complete absence of polling and reliance on secondary indicators, the forecast carries meaningful uncertainty around the exact margin, but the directional signal is unambiguous.

No public opinion polls exist for this race, the district was only redrawn in May 2026, and neither party has selected a nominee yet (primaries are August 6, 2026), all of which compel very low confidence. The race description explicitly states the newly configured TN-9 — stretching from Shelby County to Nashville suburbs after Memphis was split among three districts — is 'now considered a lean-Republican district.' Incumbent Steve Cohen is retiring, eliminating the Democrats' long-held incumbency advantage. Both parties have credible, officeholding candidates in competitive primaries (Brent Taylor/Todd Warner for Republicans; Justin Pearson/London Lamar for Democrats), which suggests both sides will field a viable general election candidate. No polling data exists to quantify the shift. The qualitative structural signal from the redistricting points to a meaningful Republican advantage, but the total absence of polling, the unsettled primaries, and the historic Democratic lean of the area under previous maps all warrant treating this as a lean Republican seat with substantial uncertainty.

Tennessee has a strong Republican lean in federal elections, and the incumbent Republican Senator Bill Hagerty is seeking re-election. There is no public polling available, but the historical context and Cook Political Report rating of Solid R indicate an overwhelming Republican advantage.

The available numeric head-to-head polling from March through May consistently shows incumbent Republican Greg Abbott leading Democrat Gina Hinojosa, generally by about 5 to 7 points, with Abbott in the high 40s and Hinojosa in the low 40s. Abbott also has the structural advantages of incumbency and Texas' recent Republican statewide lean. At the same time, the race is not out of reach for Democrats: Abbott is mostly below 50% in the cited polling, Hinojosa appears to be running competitively for a Democrat in Texas, and some listed polls do not provide usable toplines, limiting the evidence base. Third-party and independent candidates are unlikely to win but could modestly affect the final margin. Overall, the data supports a meaningful but not overwhelming Republican advantage.

Trump's 74.3% share in the district, Moran's strong two-term incumbency on the House Ways and Means Committee, and the lack of any district-level polling or fundraising data indicating competitiveness all point to an overwhelming Republican advantage. The Supreme Court-upheld redistricting maintains the district's solid conservative composition, while Democratic nominee Yolanda Prince is a first-time candidate without prior elected office.

No district-specific general election polls exist as of June 2026, so this forecast relies entirely on non-polling indicators and carries medium confidence. Cook Political Report rates TX-02 as Solid Republican. The district covers Republican-leaning northern Houston suburbs including The Woodlands, Humble, and Atascocita. Republican nominee Steve Toth is a known quantity as a sitting state representative who unseated a four-term GOP incumbent in the primary, demonstrating strong local organizing strength. Democrat Shaun Finnie is a first-time candidate with a strong professional background but no elected office history in a district that has not supported a Democratic House candidate in recent cycles. The open-seat nature and lack of polling inject some uncertainty, but the structural partisan advantage points to an overwhelming Republican advantage.

No district-specific polling is available, so confidence is limited and the forecast relies on district fundamentals rather than head-to-head data. Those fundamentals strongly favor Republicans: TX-03 has a Cook PVI of R+10, has been held by Republicans since 1968, and incumbent Keith Self is seeking a third term in a Republican-friendly map that the Supreme Court allowed Texas to use for 2026. Democrat Evan Hunt is a credible challenger with military and executive credentials, but in an R+10 district without any polling showing a shift, Republicans retain a clear and substantial advantage — though not an overwhelming one, as a strong Democratic wave could theoretically narrow the margin.

No district-specific public polling exists (only generic Texas-wide ballot polls, which are not applicable), limiting confidence. However, the structural fundamentals overwhelmingly favor Republicans: the district has a Cook PVI of R+16 and is rated 'Solid R' by Cook Political Report. Incumbent Republican Rep. Pat Fallon, first elected in 2020 and holding key committee roles (Armed Services subcommittee chair, Intelligence, Oversight), is seeking a fourth term. The Democratic challenger, Jason Pearce, is a first-time candidate with no elected office experience. The 2025 mid-decade redistricting, upheld by the U.S. Supreme Court, preserved the district's heavily Republican character. Without any contrary district-level evidence, Fallon holds an overwhelming structural advantage, though the complete absence of polling prevents high confidence and keeps the margin estimate approximate.

No district-specific polling is available, so the forecast relies entirely on structural factors. The race description states the district 'voted heavily Republican in recent cycles.' Incumbent Lance Gooden is seeking a fifth term with key committee assignments and no indicated vulnerability. Democratic nominee Chelsey Hockett is a first-time candidate with a limited public profile who won a primary runoff, and independent Dea Foy has no evident organized support. In the absence of contrary data, the district's strong Republican lean and incumbency advantage point to an overwhelming GOP hold. The lack of polling keeps confidence at medium rather than high, but the available evidence strongly supports a safe Republican rating.

No district-specific general election polling exists. This forecast relies entirely on non-polling indicators. Jake Ellzey is the Republican incumbent, first elected in a 2021 special election, who won renomination comfortably (66.3% in the March 2026 primary). Democratic nominee Danny Minton is a first-time candidate who ran unopposed for his party's nomination. Cook Political Report rates the race 'Solid Republican.' Mid-decade 2025 redistricting—upheld by the Supreme Court after a racial gerrymander challenge—introduces some uncertainty about the district's exact partisan composition, but with no polling, no signs of Democratic strength, and a strong incumbent, the evidence points to a substantial Republican advantage.

Incumbent Rep. Lizzie Fletcher holds a D+13 PVI seat and has won four consecutive elections since flipping it in 2018. The Republican nominee is a first-time candidate, and the lack of polling combined with mid-decade redistricting modestly dampens confidence but does not alter the fundamental Democratic advantage in this seat.

title: 2026 U.S. House General Election — Texas's 8th Congressional District

forecast.rationale: No district-specific polling exists for TX-08, so this forecast relies entirely on structural and historical factors. The district has a Cook PVI of R+13 and Donald Trump carried it by over 30 points in 2024 — a deeply Republican seat. Both candidates won their primaries decisively (Steinmann 68%, Jones 66%), but the district's partisan foundation gives the Republican nominee an overwhelming structural advantage. The open-seat nature introduces modest uncertainty vs. an incumbent race, but not enough to move this from a Safe Republican rating. Confidence is medium because of the total absence of district-level polling data.

The district was redrawn to favor Republicans and carries a Trump +19 baseline, placing it well beyond the competitive range. Mealer is a credible Republican nominee with prior countywide campaign experience, while no general-election polling exists to challenge the structural GOP advantage.

Texas's 10th District (R+10) provides Republicans with a strong structural advantage after McCaul's retirement, reinforced by Trump's 60%-38% performance here in 2024. Gober's dominant 51% primary win in a 10-candidate field, Trump endorsement, and deep fundraising network make him a clear favorite over Democratic nominee Rourk in this conservative-leaning open seat.

No public polling exists for this race, but structural factors overwhelmingly favor the Republican incumbent: a three-term incumbent in a district with a Cook PVI of R+17 and a nearly 10-to-1 Republican voter registration advantage faces a Democratic challenger who won a modest primary (57.6%) and an independent with no visible campaign infrastructure.

The district's R+11 PVI and 24-point Trump margin, combined with incumbent Craig Goldman's seat advantage and a Solid Republican Cook rating, point to a deeply uncompetitive race. No district-level polling exists, but structural fundamentals overwhelmingly favor the Republican incumbent.

No district-specific public polling exists for this general election matchup, which constrains confidence to 'low' despite strong structural factors. TX-13 is rated Solid Republican by Cook with a PVI of R+23, and has not elected a Democrat to Congress since the early 1990s. Incumbent Ronny Jackson won his primary with 89.5%, demonstrating strong intraparty support. While Democratic nominee Mark Nair is a credible former Amarillo City Council member, the district's deeply Republican partisan lean, incumbency advantage, and absence of any recent Democratic competitiveness in the district indicate an overwhelming Republican advantage. The margin estimate reflects the district's strong Republican skew based on historical voting patterns.

Seven-term incumbent Randy Weber holds a massive structural advantage in an R+12 district rated 'Solid Republican' by Cook, with no polling suggesting any path to competitiveness for the Democratic challenger.

Republican incumbent Monica De La Cruz holds a strong structural advantage in a district redrawn by Texas Republicans in 2025 to be more GOP-friendly, with Donald Trump having carried the current lines by 18 points in 2024. She has won the seat twice (2022, 2024) and is the first Republican to represent this district since 1903. However, the only available poll — a September 2025 House Majority PAC (Democratic-affiliated) survey — shows a close race at 41% De La Cruz to 38% Pulido with 21% undecided, suggesting more competitiveness than the partisan baseline alone would indicate. Democratic challenger Bobby Pulido brings significant name recognition as a Latin Grammy-winning Tejano musician with crossover appeal in the heavily Hispanic district. The poll is nearly 9 months old, partisan-sponsored, and lacks independent corroboration. Given the strong Republican structural edge tempered by Pulido's potential crossover strength and the sparse polling evidence, Likely Republican is the most appropriate rating, with medium confidence due to the limited and dated polling data.

No district-specific public polling is available, limiting granular confidence. However, the structural data is unambiguous: TX-16 has a Cook PVI of D+11, has not elected a Republican since 1962, features a four-term Democratic incumbent in Veronica Escobar who has never lost a congressional race, is rated 'Solid D' by Cook Political Report, and is not targeted by national Republican leadership. These fundamentals point to an overwhelming Democratic advantage with no plausible near-term competitive pathway for a Republican challenger.

No public general-election polling exists for this race as of June 2026. The forecast relies on non-polling indicators: the district was redrawn under a 2025 map described as favorable to Republicans and expected to net the GOP additional seats statewide; incumbent Republican Pete Sessions has extensive congressional experience (including as Rules Committee chair and NRCC chair) and was unopposed in the Republican primary; the Democratic nominee Casey Shepard won a competitive three-way primary and runoff but faces a heavily Republican district; and Cook Political Report rates the race as 'Solid R.' Confidence is medium rather than high due to the absence of race-specific polls.

No public general-election polls exist for this race, which reduces precision but does not alter the fundamental structural picture. The district's Cook PVI is D+29, it is rated Solid D by the Cook Political Report, and the Democratic incumbent Christian Menefee faces a Republican challenger, Ronald Whitfield, described as a perennial candidate with little public profile and no reported fundraising or campaign infrastructure. Mid-decade redistricting forced a competitive Democratic primary (Menefee defeated longtime incumbent Al Green), but the general-election configuration remains overwhelmingly Democratic. With no polling available, the forecast relies entirely on these structural factors: the district's deep-blue partisan lean, Menefee's incumbency, and Whitfield's apparent lack of campaign resources. A very high Democratic win probability is warranted, though the absence of polling data caps confidence at medium.

Texas's 19th District is an overwhelmingly Republican open seat where Trump won by 52 points in 2024, and nominee Tom Sell brings strong local credentials and agriculture policy expertise. The absence of general-election polling and the open-seat context are the main limiting factors, but the district's structural partisan advantage makes a Democratic victory extremely unlikely.

title: Texas's 20th Congressional District General Election, 2026
jurisdiction: Texas's 20th Congressional District (San Antonio and Bexar County)

forecast.rationale: TX-20 carries a D+16 Cook PVI and is San Antonio's only reliably Democratic district. Seven-term incumbent Joaquin Castro is a well-funded committee senior with zero primary opposition (88% primary vote), while Republican Edgardo Baez is a first-time candidate in a seat Democrats have held continuously since 2013.

TX-21 is a reliably Republican district where Trump won by 23 points in 2024, and Republican nominee Mark Teixeira combines elite name recognition with endorsements from Trump and Abbott, giving him a massive structural advantage over Democrat Kristin Hook and independent Dan McQueen in this open-seat race.

TX-22 is rated 'Solidly Republican' by Cook, and the 2024 general election resulted in a 24-point GOP victory (62%-38%). Republican nominee Trever Nehls benefits from near-total name recognition as the identical twin of retiring Rep. Troy Nehls, while Democrat Marquette Greene-Scott, though a credible local official, lost by the same margin in 2024, all pointing to a safe Republican hold.

TX-23's strong GOP lean (Trump +15 in 2024) and Trump's endorsement of Herrera give Republicans a structural edge in this open seat, but Herrera's controversial profile as a gun-rights YouTuber and the only poll showing a narrow 42–40 race suggest Democrats have a viable path.

There are no public polls available for this race, so the forecast relies entirely on district fundamentals, which strongly favor the incumbent Republican. Beth Van Duyne is a three-term incumbent in a district that was significantly redrawn in 2021 to favor Republicans, and she has won her previous two elections in the redrawn district by approximately 20-point margins. Cook Political Report rates the seat 'Solidly Republican.' Kevin Burge is a credible Democratic nominee (Marine Corps veteran, former White House Situation Room advisor), but in this heavily Republican-leaning district he remains a clear long-shot. The win probability of 0.97 reflects an overwhelming Republican advantage consistent with the 'safe_r' rating band (95%+). However, confidence is medium rather than high due to the complete absence of polling data and the possibility that district dynamics could shift by November.

No district-specific general election polls were found. The non-polling signals point strongly toward the Republican incumbent: Roger Williams has held the seat since 2013, chairs the House Small Business Committee, and the Cook Political Report rates the race as Solidly Republican. However, the newly enacted 2025 maps are described as 'somewhat more competitive,' and the complete absence of polling data elevates uncertainty. Dione Sims, the Democratic challenger, has a notable public profile as Dr. Opal Lee's granddaughter and a Juneteenth advocate, but no polling quantifies her support. The rating stops at likely_r (rather than safe_r) to reflect the map changes and sparse data, yielding roughly a 93% Republican win probability with low confidence.

No district-specific public polling exists for this race, which caps confidence. However, the fundamentals strongly favor the Republican incumbent: Brandon Gill is the first-term incumbent in Texas's 26th District, which is described as a strongly conservative district where Donald Trump won by 24 points in 2024. Cook Political Report rates the race as 'Solid Republican.' Gill is a Trump-aligned House Freedom Caucus member with committee assignments on Judiciary, Oversight, and Budget. Democratic nominee Steven Shook is a credible healthcare-focused challenger who won his primary, but faces a significant structural disadvantage in a district that has not elected a Democrat in decades. The Libertarian candidate Phil Gray is a perennial candidate with limited vote share. With zero polling data and strong fundamentals pointing decisively toward the incumbent, a safe Republican rating with medium confidence is the appropriate informational forecast.

No district-specific polls exist for TX-27 in 2026, but Cook Political Report rates it 'Solidly Republican,' the strongest GOP designation. Incumbent Michael Cloud, a House Freedom Caucus member seeking his fifth full term, faces Democratic challenger Tanya Lloyd, a kindergarten teacher who lacks the polling, fundraising, or district-level evidence to suggest competitiveness in this heavily Republican Gulf Coast district.

No district-specific general election polls exist for TX-28 as of June 2026, so the forecast is based entirely on non-polling indicators. Incumbent Henry Cuellar (D) has represented the district since 2005, giving him deep name recognition and institutional advantages, and Cook Political Report rates the race 'Lean Democratic.' Cuellar won his 2026 primary with 58.1%, while Republican Tano Tijerina won his primary decisively with 74.3% and has Trump's endorsement. The district in South Texas has been trending rightward, and Tijerina is a credible local officeholder (Webb County Judge) who switched parties in 2024. Cuellar's 2024 federal bribery indictment—pardoned by Trump in December 2025—adds an unusual cross-current that could either neutralize the issue or create voter confusion. Without polling to resolve these competing dynamics, Democrats appear moderately favored but the race remains competitive.

No general-election polling exists for this race as of June 2026, so the forecast is based on district fundamentals and contextual signals rather than direct matchup data. Incumbent Democrat Sylvia Garcia won a three-way Democratic primary with 58% of the vote in March 2026 despite significant mid-decade redistricting by the Republican-controlled Texas Legislature—a redraw designed to make the seat more competitive by moving many Latino voters out and adding more Black voters. However, Cook Political Report still rates the seat as 'Solid D,' and the race description characterizes Garcia as heavily favored. The absence of a serious funded challenge (Fierro ran uncontested in the Republican primary) and Garcia's strong primary performance amid unfavorable map changes suggest the district's Democratic lean remains intact for now. Confidence is medium because the lack of general-election polling and the untested electoral effects of the 2025 redistricting introduce genuine uncertainty that cannot be resolved with the available data.

Texas's 30th District has a Cook PVI of D+25 and a long history of Democratic dominance. Frederick Haynes III is a well-known local figure with strong institutional support including the retiring incumbent's endorsement, while Republican Everett Jackson faces severe structural headwinds in this district.

No public general-election polls exist in the provided race data. The forecast is based solely on structural factors: Cook Political Report rates the race Solid Republican, the district has a Partisan Voting Index of R+11, and incumbent John Carter has held the seat for 24 years (since the district's creation in 2003). Carter won a crowded primary with nearly 60% of the vote, indicating durable base support. Democrat Justin Early is a credible challenger (Army veteran, cybersecurity professional) and won his primary with 57.6%, but faces steep structural headwinds in a district that has not elected a Democrat to Congress. The incumbent's age (84) introduces some uncertainty not captured by fundamentals alone, but absent any polling or race-specific evidence of vulnerability, the district's Republican lean and long incumbency make a GOP hold overwhelming. Confidence is medium rather than high due to zero public polling and the unusual age factor.

No public polling exists in this race, limiting quantitative confidence. Structurally, however, the district was redrawn in August 2025 from D+22 to R+17, a massive 39-point swing toward Republicans. The incumbent Democratic representative opted to run in the neighboring 33rd district rather than defend this redrawn seat, leaving this an open seat. The Republican nominee Jace Yarbrough has received endorsements from President Donald Trump and other major conservative figures, while the Democratic nominee Dan Barrios is a Richardson City Councilmember. The race description explicitly calls this a top Republican pickup opportunity. An R+17 lean combined with strong incumbency/endorsement signals gives Republicans a clear structural advantage. However, absence of any polling and the inherent uncertainty of a newly configured district caution against a safe rating.

TX-33 has a Cook PVI of D+18 and is rated 'Solid D' by Cook Political Report, giving Democrats an overwhelming structural advantage even after mid-decade redistricting. Democrat Colin Allred is a well-funded former congressman with strong name ID, while Republican Patrick Gillespie previously lost this seat by 27 points in 2024.

This race is a true tossup based on the available data. The only public poll is a single NRCC-commissioned survey from April 2026 showing Eric Flores at 41% and Vicente Gonzalez at 40%, a negligible 1-point gap within any standard margin of error. However, because this is a partisan-sponsored poll and no independent nonpartisan public polling exists, its evidentiary value is limited. Structural factors cut both ways: the district voted for Trump in 2024 yet re-elected Gonzalez narrowly, and Flores has high-profile endorsements (Trump, Abbott) while Gonzalez is a sitting moderate incumbent and Blue Dog co-chair who has demonstrated crossover appeal. With only one partisan poll at this stage and mixed fundamental signals, the race is best characterized as a tossup with high uncertainty, leaning very slightly toward the incumbent by virtue of incumbency and proven ability to hold the seat.

title: Texas's 35th Congressional District election, 2026
jurisdiction: Texas's 35th Congressional District — Bexar, Guadalupe, Wilson, and Karnes counties

forecast.rationale: 2025 redistricting reconfigured TX-35 to favor Republicans, with Trump carrying the new lines by ~10 points and Cook rating it R+4, giving Carlos De La Cruz a structural advantage in this open-seat race. However, the district is Hispanic-majority and includes parts of San Antonio, offering Democrat Johnny Garcia a viable coalitional path, and zero public polling keeps the uncertainty elevated.

No district-specific public polling exists for this race, which limits confidence to medium. However, the structural data strongly favors the incumbent. Brian Babin is a six-term incumbent (first elected 2014) and current Chairman of the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee. He won his 2026 primary with 81.1% of the vote. The district's Cook PVI is R+12 and the 2025 redistricting maintained its strongly Republican tilt. The only broader polling signal—a June 2026 Texas generic ballot showing Republicans ahead 49% to 43%—is consistent with a Republican advantage. Rhonda Hart is a credible Democratic nominee (Army veteran and gun-safety activist) and won her primary with 64.1%, but the district's partisan lean combined with Babin's incumbency and fundraising/chairship advantages make the Republican nominee a clear favorite. A likely_r rating (92% win probability, ~17-point margin estimate) reflects that the seat is not quite safe—a Democratic longshot win is possible if national dynamics shift dramatically—but Babin holds a commanding structural edge.
